title: Home & everyday objects
goal: Describe a home, say where things are (on, under, inside, near) and say what there is and isn't.
intro: Location in Odia is expressed with the ending **-ରେ** (*-re*) 'in/at/on' and with **postpositions** that come *after* the noun: ଟେବୁଲ **ଉପରେ** 'on the table' (literally *table on*). With **ଅଛି / ନାହିଁ** you can then say what there is and isn't.

vocab.note: ମୋ ପାଖରେ ଟଙ୍କା ନାହିଁ 'I don't have money on me'.

grammar.title: Location: -ରେ and postpositions
grammar.body:
The locative ending **-ରେ** (*-re*) means 'in, at, on': କୋଠରୀରେ 'in the room', ଟେବୁଲରେ 'on the table', କଟକରେ 'in Cuttack'. A few common nouns ending in -ô take just **-ଏ** instead: ଘର → **ଘରେ** 'at home'.

More precise positions use **postpositions** placed after the noun (the noun may optionally take -ର): ଟେବୁଲ **ଉପରେ** 'on top of the table', ଖଟ **ତଳେ** 'under the bed', ବ୍ୟାଗ **ଭିତରେ** 'inside the bag', ଘର **ବାହାରେ** 'outside the house', ମୋ **ପାଖରେ** 'near me', ଦୁଆର **ଆଗରେ** 'in front of the door', ଘର **ପଛରେ** 'behind the house'.

Swap the final -ରେ for **-କୁ** to show movement *towards* (ଭିତରକୁ 'into'), or **-ରୁ** for *from* (ଭିତରୁ 'from inside', ଘରୁ 'from home').

examples.en: The key is on the table.
The cat is under the bed.
My phone is in the bag.

examples.native: ଆମ ଘର ପଛରେ ଗୋଟିଏ ପୋଖରୀ ଅଛି।
examples.roman: amô ghôrô pôchhôre goṭie pokhôri ôchhi.
examples.en: There's a pond behind our house.

grammar.title: 'There is / there are': ଅଛି and ନାହିଁ
grammar.body:
**ଅଛି** means 'there is/are' and **ନାହିଁ** 'there isn't/aren't' — the same for singular and plural things. For people, use the respectful **ଅଛନ୍ତି / ନାହାନ୍ତି**. The place usually comes first: *In the room two windows there-are.*

To ask, use rising intonation or add **କି**: ଏଠି ୱାଇଫାଇ ଅଛି କି? 'Is there wifi here?' **କେହି** 'anyone' and **କିଛି** 'anything' with ନାହିଁ give 'no one' and 'nothing'.

examples.en: There are two windows in the room.
There's no curd in the fridge.

dialogue.title: Looking at a room to rent
dialogue.setting: Sam is shown a room by the landlord, Mr Mohanty.

lines.speaker: Mr Mohanty
lines.en: Come in, this is the room.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ବାଃ, ଦୁଇଟି ଝରକା ଅଛି। ପଙ୍ଖା ବି ଅଛି।
lines.roman: baḥ, duiṭi jhôrôka ôchhi. pôṅkha bi ôchhi.
lines.en: Nice, there are two windows. And a fan too.

lines.speaker: Mr Mohanty
lines.native: ହଁ। ଖଟ, ଟେବୁଲ, ଚେୟାର, ଆଲମାରୀ — ସବୁ ଅଛି।
lines.roman: hôṃ. khôṭô, ṭebulô, cheyarô, almari — sôbu ôchhi.
lines.en: Yes. Bed, table, chair, cupboard — everything's here.

lines.speaker: Mr Mohanty
lines.native: ବାରଣ୍ଡା ପାଖରେ। ଆଉ ବାଥରୁମ୍ କୋଠରୀ ଭିତରେ।
lines.roman: barôṇḍa pakhôre. au bathrum koṭhôri bhitôre.
lines.en: Next to the veranda. And the bathroom is inside the room.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: Is there water 24 hours a day?

lines.speaker: Mr Mohanty
lines.en: Yes, there's a tank on the roof.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: Okay. I'll think it over and let you know.

culture: Shoes come off at the door of an Odia home, and always before entering the kitchen or the family's prayer corner (ଠାକୁର ଘର). Many houses have a flat roof (ଛାତ) used for drying clothes, pickles and papad, and for sleeping out on hot nights. A guest is usually offered water and something sweet straight away.
